topic: Functional hierarchy of movement check
idea: Trips pass through six stages (main movement, transition, distribution, collection, access, termination); obsolescence arises when a high-speed arterial or freeway ramp connects directly to a large generator/local street without a transition facility. Check each junction pair for jumps of more than one functional class (e.g. freeway ramp meeting a local street) and speed-limit steps larger than a stated amount.
does: Flags roads/junctions where adjacent roads differ by more than one functional step or speed step (fast arterial straight into local/access road), and institutions whose door sits on a high-speed road.
inputs: road speed, lanes, road type label, institution doors
outputs: list of hierarchy breaks with suggested transition (collector, slip lane, speed step)
existing: partial: analyse_network (design check, no hierarchy)
notes: Road type label is a stored-only placeholder in ACMS, so classes would be inferred from speed/lanes.

topic: Design hour volume (K and D factors)
idea: Design volume is not ADT but the 30th highest hourly volume (30HV, about 15% of ADT rural, K 8-12% urban); directional design hour volume DDHV = ADT x K x D (D 55-70% peak direction, up to 80%). Lanes needed per direction follow from DDHV (example 4,000 veh/h two-way, 80% directional needs 3,200 veh/h one way). Intersection design needs the AM and PM turning movements separately.
does: From the demand's daily curve or trips/day, computes K (peak-hour share), D (directional split) and DDHV per boundary pair/road, ranks the Nth busiest hour (30th-hour analogue from the 24 h curve), and tells which roads would need more lanes at a veh/h/lane criterion; runs the sim at the design hour rather than the average hour.
inputs: daily OD trips, daily curve, optional K and D overrides, lane count, per-lane capacity criterion
outputs: per road/direction: DHV, DDHV, K, D, lanes required vs present, recommended design hour for run_simulation
existing: partial: shape_daily_curve, scale_demand (to degree_of_saturation), read_od_matrix
notes: ACMS has a 24 h curve so K is measurable directly; AASHTO typical values (K 0.15 rural, 0.08-0.12 urban, D 0.55-0.70) are the defaults when no curve.

topic: Range-based demand forecast sensitivity
idea: Because forecasts are uncertain (design period 15-24 years, 20 typical), evaluate a design under lower and upper bound traffic forecasts and report the sensitivity, even if the design does not change.
does: Runs the same design across a low/central/high demand scale (e.g. 0.8/1.0/1.2 of design-year demand) with paired seeds and reports the KPI sensitivity and the scale at which a link or junction breaks down (queue spill, degree of saturation > 1).
inputs: scenario, low/high scale factors, seeds
outputs: KPI by demand bound, breakdown scale, regression slope of delay on demand
existing: partial: run_experiment (scenarios scale demand) and scale_demand
notes: Mostly a recipe on run_experiment plus a breakdown-point search (bisection on demand_scale).

topic: Driver reaction time with expectancy
idea: Brake reaction time averages 0.6 s for expected events (some up to 2 s) and +35% for unexpected (up to 2.7 s); reaction time grows with information bits (Fig 2-1 median, Fig 2-2 85th percentile). Older drivers: slower processing, more crashes making left turns, merging, gap acceptance.
does: Vehicle driver profile with a reaction time distribution (expected 0.6 s mean, unexpected x1.35) and an older-driver class with larger tau and more conservative gap acceptance, so safety/TTC and capacity experiments can compare driver mixes.
inputs: driver class shares, reaction time mean and tail
outputs: per-vehicle tau/sigma/gap parameters; conflict and capacity effects by driver mix
existing: none
notes: Krauss tau is the lever; AASHTO SSD uses 2.5 s design reaction (see Ch 3).

topic: Design speed table and operating speed (85th percentile)
idea: Low-speed design is up to 45 mph [70 km/h], high speed from 50 mph [80 km/h]; operating speed is the 85th percentile of free-flow speeds; running speed = section length / travel time. Target speed concept: posted speed in walkable urban areas set to the desired operating speed. Features affecting operating speed: curve radius, grade, access density, median, parking, signal density, volume, ped/bike activity.
does: Compares each road's posted speed with the measured 85th-percentile operating speed from detectors and with the curve-radius-safe speed; flags roads where operating speed exceeds the target/design speed, and where adjacent roads' speeds differ by more than 20 km/h.
inputs: run detectors (85th percentile speeds), road posted speeds, curve radii
outputs: per road: posted, V85, design/curve speed, excess, speed-step flags between neighbours
existing: partial: read_detectors (15/50/85th percentile speeds), analyse_network (curve posted too fast)
notes: Speed-step (consistency) rule of about 10 mph between successive elements appears in Ch 3; combine there.

topic: Access density screening
idea: Crash rate rises about 3% per added access point per mile (about 5% per access point per km); 20 to 50 access points/mile nearly doubles crashes; non-traversable median < two-way left-turn lane < undivided at all densities (Fig 2-7 urban, 2-8 rural); Fig 2-9 gives rate by unsignalised access density and signals per mile; each added signal per mile cuts speed 2-3 mph (5-8 km/h per signal per km); fully access-controlled roads have 25-50% of the crash rate.
does: Counts access points (junction legs, institution doors, bus-bay openings) and signals per km along each road/corridor and returns a relative crash index and expected speed penalty, so the assistant can rank corridors and argue for closing access or adding a median.
inputs: network roads, junction control types, institution doors, median flag (optional)
outputs: per road/corridor: access points per km, signals per km, relative crash multiplier (1 + 0.05 per access point above a baseline), speed penalty km/h, ranked list
existing: none (analyse_safety is surrogate-based on a run, not geometry)
notes: Coefficients are a literature synthesis (NCHRP 420 / Gluck et al), US data; label as indicative. Pairs with analyse_safety to compare predicted vs simulated conflicts.

topic: Design level of service by functional class and peak hour factor
idea: Customary design LOS (Table 2-3): freeway B (rural level) to C; arterial B/C rural, C/D urban; collector C/D; local D. Peak hour factor PHF = hourly volume / (4 x peak 15-min count), 0.75-0.95; design service flow rate must be at least the peak 15-minute rate (example 4,200 veh/h 15-min rate x PHF 0.80 = 3,360 veh/h). Capacity is dominated by signalised intersections on urban arterials; a 5 mph (10 km/h) speed drop is tolerable in weaving sections.
does: From a run (or the demand curve) computes the PHF from 5/15-min counts per road, and grades each road/junction against a design-LOS target by its class (speed or delay thresholds), flagging links worse than target.
inputs: run id, road class or speed, target LOS table
outputs: PHF per road, 15-min peak flow rate, LOS letter vs target, pass/fail
existing: partial: analyse_run (reliability), read_detectors (flow); not_built lists level of service
notes: LOS letter thresholds come from HCM (density for freeways, speed ratio for arterials, delay for signals) not from this book; Green Book supplies the targets only.

topic: Pedestrian walking speed and crossing time
idea: Design walking speed 3.5 ft/s (1.1 m/s), 3.0 ft/s (0.9 m/s) where older pedestrians; MUTCD: clearance (flashing don't walk) at 1.1 m/s curb to curb; total walk + clearance at 0.9 m/s from ramp to far curb. Wider streets need longer gaps and take green from vehicles; refuge islands allow two-stage crossings. 80% of pedestrian trips under 1 km, nobody walks over 1.5 km to work or 1 km to a bus; pedestrian volume peaks at noon.
does: For every signalised crossing computes the required pedestrian clearance time from the crossed carriageway width (lanes x lane width + median) at 1.1 and 0.9 m/s and compares with the signal's actual cross-phase green+amber+all-red; for unsignalised crossings gives the minimum acceptable gap and the vehicle gap it needs.
inputs: crossings, lane counts and widths, signal timings
outputs: required vs available pedestrian time per crossing, shortfall in s, suggested min green
existing: partial: describe (crossings), analyse_network
notes: Also a calibration input for institutions' walk catchments (walk limit about 1 km).

topic: Weaving section limits
idea: Weaving sections (merge then diverge with crossing paths) have a volume limit that depends on the split of weaving movements, section length and number of lanes; HCM gives a running speed equation; tolerable speed loss 10 km/h below the roadway's speed.
does: Detects weaving sections in built interchanges/ramp pairs (entry followed by exit within a short distance on the same carriageway) and compares length and lane count with the weaving demand from the OD routes.
inputs: interchange geometry, route flows through ramp pairs
outputs: weave length, weaving volume ratio, flag if length insufficient
existing: partial: build_interchange (no weaving diagnosis)
notes: The numerical weaving equation is in the HCM, not this text.

topic: Design vehicle turning-radius check at junctions
idea: Table 2-4/2-5 give 20 design vehicles with dimensions and minimum turning radii (m): P 7.26 design radius (CTR 6.40, inside 4.39); SU-9 12.73; city bus 12.80 (CTR 11.53, inside 7.45); BUS-12 12.70; articulated bus A-BUS 12.00 (inside 6.49, length 18.29); WB-12 12.16 (inside 5.88); WB-20 13.66 (inside 0.59 m, CTR 12.50); WB-20D 13.67. Radii valid below 15 km/h; CTR = min design radius minus half front width; centerline radius from steering: R = wheelbase / sin(max steering angle) (Fig 2-20). Offtracking and swept path width grow with kingpin-to-rear-axle distance. Design vehicle choice rule: WB-20 minimum on ramp terminals and truck routes, city bus/WB-12 on collector and local streets, S-BUS 11/12 on low-volume roads.
does: For every junction turn (and slip road, roundabout entry) computes the geometric corner/turn radius from the polylines and compares it with the minimum turning radius of the design vehicles actually in the vehicle types (bus, truck, trailer) or the recommended design vehicle by road class; lists turns a bus/semi cannot make without swinging into the opposing lane and the radius or lane widening needed. Also sets each vehicle type's length, width and turn speed limit from the table.
inputs: junction geometry and turn radii, vehicle types in use (or chosen design vehicle), lane width
outputs: per turn: radius available vs required, offtracking width, pass/fail, suggested curb radius
existing: partial: analyse_network (curve speed vs radius, roundabout size), list_vehicle_types
notes: Quasi-static check in metres, no vehicle swept-path animation needed. Library of 20 vehicles also feeds create_vehicle_types (articulated bus 18.3 m x 2.6 m, double trailer WB-20D 22 m).

topic: Design-vehicle library for vehicle types
idea: Overall length, width, height, front/rear overhang, wheelbase per design vehicle (Table 2-4 metric): P 5.79x2.13, SU-9 9.14x2.44, CITY-BUS 12.19x2.59, A-BUS 18.29x2.59, WB-12 13.87x2.44, WB-19 21.03x2.59, WB-20 22.40x2.59, WB-20D 29.67 (Rocky Mtn double WB-28D) etc.
does: Adds AASHTO design vehicles as presets alongside SUMO defaults in create_vehicle_types, so truck/bus dimensions used in the sim match design practice and the turning-path check.
inputs: design vehicle symbol
outputs: vehicle type with length_m, width_m, min turning radius
existing: partial: create_vehicle_types (SUMO defaults for bus, truck, trailer)
notes: Overlaps SUMO vClass defaults; useful mainly to drive the turn check.

topic: HSM six-step safety management workflow with CMFs
idea: HSM Part B process: network screening, diagnosis, countermeasure selection, economic appraisal, priority ranking, effectiveness evaluation; Part C predicts crash frequency/severity per design alternative; Part D is a catalogue of crash modification factors (CMF, multiplicative effect of a feature on crash frequency). Findings: crash frequency rises nonlinearly with volume; severity follows speed and collision type; full access control gives Interstates 30-76% of conventional-highway crash rates; the number of crashes rises with the number of driver decisions.
does: Pipeline over analyse_safety: rank roads/junctions by conflict rate (screening), diagnose dominant conflict type and cause (speed, queue spill, turning), propose countermeasures from a small CMF table (e.g. roundabout, protected left phase, speed reduction, access closure) with expected crash multiplier, re-simulate each as a scenario (run_experiment) and rank by conflicts avoided per cost.
inputs: run id for screening, CMF table, candidate edits
outputs: ranked sites, diagnosis, countermeasure list with CMF and simulated conflict change, priority order
existing: partial: analyse_safety (surrogate conflicts per road), run_experiment (compares scenarios)
cite: Ch 2 s2.9.2-2.9.4 (HSM Parts B, C, D)
notes: CMF values themselves are in the HSM/CMF Clearinghouse, not this book; the book gives the process. Speed-vs-severity link supports weighting conflicts by speed difference.

topic: Design acceleration and deceleration performance
idea: Fig 2-33 passenger car acceleration (distance to reach a speed from an initial speed on level ground, lower-performance compact car) and Fig 2-34 deceleration distances approaching intersections (comfortable rate vs minimum braking, dry vs wet pavement); governs intersection, ramp, climbing lane and bus bay dimensions. Design values deliberately represent lower-performance vehicles (loaded truck/bus).
does: Compares the simulated vehicles' accel/decel (Krauss a and b per type) against these design curves and reports speed-distance from standstill and braking distances for each type, flagging types more aggressive than the design vehicle.
inputs: vehicle type accel/decel parameters
outputs: distance to reach V from rest, braking distance from V at comfortable and max rates, comparison with Fig 2-33/2-34 values
existing: none
notes: The numeric curves are graphs only here; Ch 3 and Ch 9/10 give tabulated acceleration/deceleration lengths.

topic: Stopping and decision sight distance check
idea: SSD = 0.278 V t + V^2 / (254 (a/9.81 +/- G)) with t = 2.5 s brake reaction and a = 3.4 m/s2 (Eq 3-1 to 3-3; V km/h, G grade as fraction, minus on upgrade). Table 3-1 design SSD (m): 20 km/h 20, 40 50?, 50 km/h 65? (calc 18.5 at 20, 31.2 at 30 ... 60 km/h 85, 80 km/h 130, 100 km/h 185, 120 km/h 250 approx); Table 3-2 gives grade corrections (3/6/9%). Decision sight distance (Table 3-3, Eq 3-4/3-5) for complex decisions: avoidance A stop rural t=3 s, B stop urban t=9.1 s, C-E speed/path change t 10.2-14.5 s; at 60 km/h A 70 m, B 155, C 145, D 170, E 195; at 100 km/h 185/315/290/335/375 approx. Required at lane drops, ramp terminals, signal approaches and roundabout entries.
does: Computes required SSD and DSD from each road's speed limit (and grade if known) and compares it with the visible length along the drawn polyline: horizontal curves (offset from inside lane to a clear line of sight, Eq 3-37 HSO = R(1 - cos(28.65 S / R))), distance from last bend to a stop line/roundabout entry/merge, and distance between successive decision points (junction spacing under the DSD). Flags approaches where a driver cannot stop for a queue or a red signal.
inputs: road polylines, speed limits, junction control types, curve radii, lane offset, optional grade
outputs: per road/approach: required SSD/DSD, available sight length, margin, flags
existing: partial: analyse_network (curve posted speed vs radius) and describe (curve radius, safe speed); no sight distance
notes: Pure vector geometry in metres: sample the polyline, test visibility to a point S metres ahead with eye 1.08 m, object 0.60 m (stopping) or 1.08 m (intersection); only plan-view obstructions (other roads, institutions as building footprints) since ACMS has no profile. Also gives the simulation a way to explain rear-end conflicts at blind approaches (analyse_safety TTC).

topic: Speed-dependent side friction in curve speed
idea: Basic curve equation 0.01 e + f = V^2 / (127 R) (Eq 3-6/3-7; V km/h, R m). Design side friction f falls with speed: 0.40 at 15 km/h, 0.35 at 30?, 0.21 at 30 km/h, 0.18 at 40-50, 0.15 at 55-80 (ball-bank 14/12/10 deg), 0.16 at up to 100 km/h, 0.10 at 110+ km/h and 0.07 at 140 km/h; wet-tyre skid supply is 0.5 at 30 km/h falling to 0.35 at 100 km/h (Fig 3-3, 3-4); five methods distribute e and f over curve radius (Fig 3-5), Method 5 the curvilinear one AASHTO uses.
does: Replace the single constant (SUPERELEVATION + SIDE_FRICTION) in curve_speed_kmh with f(V) from Fig 3-4 solved iteratively, with e chosen by the Method 5 curvilinear rule or by emax per context (rural 6-12%, urban 4-6%), and an optional wet/dry margin for trucks (lower friction, rollover threshold).
inputs: curve radius, emax (context), vehicle class
outputs: safe curve speed per vehicle class, margin against posted speed, advisory speed
existing: partial: curve_speed_kmh in interchanges.py uses constant superelevation and side friction
notes: Vehicles in ACMS slow for curvature already; this would let buses/trucks slow earlier than cars and make the check agree with design practice at low speeds (urban streets).

topic: Passing sight distance and no-passing zone share
idea: Passing sight distance (Table 3-4): 120 m at 50 km/h, 180 at 80, 245 at 100, 355 at 120 (Glennon and Hassan models: speed difference 19 km/h, abort perception 1 s, decel 3.4 m/s2, headway 1 s, clearance 1 s). HCM link: 40% no-passing share raises time-spent-following up to 19% and cuts speed 3.1 km/h at 800 veh/h; passing sections shorter than 120-240 m (Table 3-5) are ignored.
does: For two-lane two-way roads without a passing lane, measures the percentage of length where available sight distance exceeds the passing minimum and predicts the loss in speed/following time.
inputs: road polylines, speed, flow
outputs: percent passing zone, penalty to speed and percent time following
existing: none
notes: ACMS vehicles do not overtake via the opposing lane, so this only informs a design check.

topic: Turning roadway / compound curve consistency check
idea: For turning roadways (ramps, slip roads, intersection curves): design speed 15 km/h minimum radius turns at intersections, higher with approach speed; compound curves should have flatter-to-sharper radius ratio not above 2:1 (about 10 km/h average running speed drop between the two curves); successive sharper curves must be long enough to decelerate at most 5 km/h per second at intersections (3 km/h/s desirable; engine braking alone gives 1.5-2.5 km/h/s) (Table 3-14 minimum arc lengths); spiral length from a 4 s maneuver time at design speed; low-speed urban streets use Method 2 (all lateral force by friction, f 0.40 at 15 km/h to 0.15 at 70 km/h) and Table 3-13 radii; superelevation runoff Lr = w n1 ed bw / delta with relative gradient 1:200 at 80+ km/h, 1:175 at 70, 1:150 at 50, 1:125 at 30.
does: For slip roads, interchange ramps and roundabout approaches built by the assistant (curve point lists), segments the curvature profile into arcs, checks radius ratios between consecutive arcs (2:1 limit), that each arc is long enough for the speed drop from the previous one at 3-5 km/h/s, and that the posted/target speed on the ramp matches the sharpest arc.
inputs: curve polyline of the road, speed limit, lane width
outputs: per curve: arcs with radius and length, ratio flags, required vs available deceleration length, advisory speed
existing: partial: build_interchange/add_slip_road (spiral clothoid, curve_speed_kmh); analyse_network curve speed vs radius
notes: Deceleration limit also sets how far upstream a vehicle model must begin braking for a curve: a check that the Krauss braking for curve speed does not exceed 3 km/h/s comfort.

topic: Lane width needed on turning roadways and curves
idea: Turning roadway width W = U + C + Z (Case I one lane, no passing: C 1.2 m, Z 0.6 m); Case II one lane with passing of a stalled vehicle: W = U1 + U2 + 2C + FA + FB with C = 0.6 m; Case III two-lane: all elements. U is track width of the design vehicle on the curve (includes offtracking), FA front overhang. Curve widening Eq 3-36: Wc = N(U + C) + (N-1)FA + Z. Table 3-26b (inner-edge radius 15 m, Case I): P 4.0 m, SU-9 5.5, city bus 7.2, A-BUS 6.7, WB-12 6.5, WB-20 13.5 m; tangent 3.6-4.4 m. Table 3-27 gives design widths for traffic conditions A (mostly cars), B (5-10% trucks), C (buses/semis), with edge corrections (vertical curb adds 0.3-0.6 m, stabilized shoulder deducts).
does: Compares the lane width available on slip roads, ramps and tight turns with the width needed by the vehicle mix (share of trucks/buses in the OD demand and fleet) for the radius, returning the needed width and where trucks would encroach into the adjacent lane (which also slows the sim: trucks crossing lane lines).
inputs: turn radius, lane width, vehicle type shares from demand and vehicle types
outputs: required width by case and traffic condition, deficit, flag
existing: none
notes: Same input as check_turning_paths (SRC_022-010); implement as one check.

topic: Road grade, truck speed profile and climbing lane warrant
idea: Vertical alignment is absent in ACMS. Add a per-road grade; heavy truck (weight/power 120 kg/kW, 85-120) climbs at reduced speed per Fig 3-16 to 3-19 (speed-distance curves); critical length of grade = length of an upgrade that cuts a truck's speed 15 km/h below traffic's average running speed (Fig 3-21; e.g. 4% upgrade, 350 m; 6% after a 4% downgrade 370 m); max grades about 5% at 110 km/h to 7-12% at 50 km/h; Truck Speed Profile Model (TSPM) takes weight/power, initial speed and a grade sequence. Climbing lane warrant (all three): upgrade flow over 200 veh/h, upgrade trucks over 20 veh/h, and one of (10 mph/15 km/h truck speed loss expected, LOS E/F on grade, two-level LOS drop approach to grade); flow rate = DHV x D / PHF. Crash involvement of a truck rises 2.4x when its speed deficit goes from 10 to 15 mph.
does: Gives each road an optional grade and each truck/bus type a weight/power ratio so the sim slows heavy vehicles uphill (power-limited acceleration a = (P/m)/v - g(G + f)), reports critical length of grade exceeded, queues behind slow trucks, and tests the climbing-lane warrant from the demand (upgrade flow, truck flow, speed reduction) in analyse_network.
inputs: road grade profile (percent per segment), truck weight/power, approach speed, DHV, D, PHF
outputs: truck speed profile along the road, critical length, warrant verdict, simulated delay with and without a climbing lane (extra lane scenario)
existing: none (not_built: road types do not change behaviour; no vertical profile)
notes: Needs a new road attribute (grade) and a vehicle-power model; the editor and Krauss model are 2D-flat today. Smaller version: grade as a speed/accel multiplier per vehicle class.

topic: Speed-differential crash involvement
idea: Crash involvement rate rises with how far a vehicle's speed deviates below (or above) the traffic average (Fig 3-20): truck involvement rate rises about 2.4x going from a 10 mph to a 15 mph deficit; the average speed of all traffic falls about 30% of the truck speed loss.
does: Adds a speed-differential indicator to analyse_safety: per road, share of vehicle-km driven more than 15 km/h below the mean (slow trucks, buses at stops) or above, and a relative risk index using the 2.4x step at 15 km/h.
inputs: run detectors speed distributions per road, vehicle class
outputs: per road: standard deviation of speed, share of slow outliers, relative involvement index
existing: partial: analyse_safety (rear-end TTC conflicts), read_detectors (percentile speeds)
notes: Complements the TTC surrogate with a speed-variance risk indicator.

topic: Frontage road and median treatments for access control
idea: Frontage roads segregate local traffic from through traffic: one-way preferred, continuous parallel at about 50 m from the arterial in urban areas, connections near crossroads, slip ramps to two-way frontage roads cause wrong-way entry; raised/non-traversable medians (6 ft = 1.8 m minimum as pedestrian refuge) cut conflicts but divert left turns to U-turns downstream; two-way left-turn lane works at 3.0-4.8 m median width and reduces rear-end crashes but increases access opportunities; median table 4-2 countermeasures (barrier, wider median, avoid radii under 900 m).
does: Assistant tool that builds a parallel one-way frontage (service) road beside a selected arterial at a given offset (default 50 m) with connections at the junctions, and re-points institution doors onto it, so access density on the arterial drops; then run_experiment can compare delay and conflicts.
inputs: road id, side, offset_m, connection junctions, one-way flag
outputs: new roads, rerouted door junctions, before/after access density
existing: none (add_road, add_slip_road exist; no frontage generator)
notes: Pairs with access_density_screen (SRC_022-006).

topic: Bus bay and stop geometry rules
idea: Arterial bus turnout: deceleration taper about 5:1, loading area 15 m per bus x 3.0-3.6 m wide, re-entry taper not sharper than 3:1; minimum total turnout length for a two-bus bay 60 m midblock, 45 m near-side, 42 m far-side (add 3.9-4.8 m for 3.6 m width); boarding area 2.4 m deep x 1.5 m wide, cross slope under 2%; far-side stops use the intersection as entry area. Park-and-ride: bus roadway width at least 6 m to pass a standing bus, sawtooth arrangement when more than 2 buses (parallel bay 29 m for two buses, +14 m each extra), access 90 m from other intersections, one entrance/exit per 500 spaces.
does: Checks every bus stop for bay length vs number of buses that dwell at once (headways x dwell from vehicle types), clearance from the junction (near-side/far-side), taper space, and flags stops where queued buses would block the through lane (bay shorter than needed); suggests moving to far-side or lengthening.
inputs: bus stops (distance along road, direction, dwell_s), bus headways, junction positions
outputs: per stop: buses present at once (arrival rate x dwell), required bay length, available length, placement class and flag
existing: partial: add_bus_stop/update_bus_stop (bay beside kerb, clear of junctions); no bay length or capacity check
notes: Number of berths needed also follows from buses/h x dwell (TCRP 100 methods, not in this text); here only geometry.

topic: On-street parking effect on capacity
idea: On-street parking decreases through capacity, impedes flow and raises crash potential; parking lane 2.4 m (3.0-3.6 m if used as through lane in peak or by transit); local street 7.8 m wide with parking both sides keeps one through lane; end the parking lane about 6 m before intersections so right-turners do not use it.
does: Optional on-street parking attribute per road side that adds friction: parked vehicles' manoeuvres block the kerb lane for random intervals, reduce effective lane width, and the tool compares delay/crash conflicts with parking removed (peak-hour clearway scenario).
inputs: road side, parking occupancy/turnover, lane width
outputs: capacity change, delay, conflicts; scenario pair for run_experiment
existing: none (not_built lists nothing on parking)
notes: Source gives no capacity numbers (HCM does); keep it a clearly labelled placeholder per AGENTS.md.

topic: Design criteria compliance by road class (local streets)
idea: Urban local street criteria: design speed 30-50 km/h (encourage under 50); lane width 3.0-3.3 m (2.7 m minimum residential, 3.6 m industrial); minimum horizontal radius the greater of 30 m or the Table 3-7 radius for the design speed; SSD 30-60 m; grades under 15% residential, under 8% commercial; superelevation usually none (max 4%, 6%); turn lanes at least 2.7 m (desirably 3.0-3.6 m); 7.8-8 m roadway with parking both sides gives one 3.6 m through lane; cul-de-sacs and turnarounds sized by the design vehicle (fire truck, refuse).
does: A compliance check by functional class: from each road's class (inferred from speed/lanes or a label) and context (urban/suburban/rural from institution density) compares speed limit, lane width, curve radius, SSD, junction spacing and number of lanes with the Green Book ranges and lists violations with the cited value, as analyse_network does for curve speed.
inputs: network roads, road class label or inferred class, context
outputs: per road: criteria table row, actual values, violations, suggested edit (reduce speed limit, widen lane, flatten curve)
existing: partial: analyse_network (validity, short roads, curve speed vs radius, roundabout size)
notes: Collector/arterial/freeway criteria added from SRC_022 Ch 6-8 chunks; the road type label is stored-only in ACMS today so classification would be inferred.

topic: Context-sensitive target speed from land use
idea: Five contexts by development density, land use and setback (rural, rural town, suburban, urban, urban core) with arterial design speed ranges: rural level terrain 80-120 km/h, rural town 30-70, suburban 50-90, urban 40-70, urban core 50 or less; collectors rural minimum design speed by terrain and volume (Table 6-1: level 60/80/100 km/h for under 400/400-2000/over 2000 veh/day); rural-town entry needs a transition zone (perception-reaction area then deceleration area) with staged speed limits and physical treatments (islands, narrowing, roundabouts). Target speed = the posted limit and desired operating speed.
does: Classifies each road's context from the density of institutions (people, floor area, doors) and junction density within a buffer of the road, then recommends a target speed range by functional class and flags roads whose posted speed or measured V85 exceeds it, plus abrupt speed-limit drops between connected roads needing a transition (staged limits).
inputs: institutions (centre, area, people), junction spacing, road speed limits, run V85
outputs: context class per road, recommended speed range, over-limit flags, suggested staged limits
existing: partial: analyse_network (curve posted speed); list_institutions has the density data
notes: Gives ACMS a way to use its institutions as land-use context; NCHRP 855 (context classification) and NCHRP 737 (transition zones) are the underlying studies.

topic: Reversible (tidal) lane warrant and dynamic reversal
idea: A reverse-flow roadway serving opposite directions at different times is warranted when peak directional split is substantially unbalanced (about 65:35) and capacity analysis would need more than 8 lanes conventionally, when parallel facilities are not feasible, and when much of the peak-direction traffic is long distance with few intervening exits (Fig 8-18, 8-19); the central roadway is closed twice a day to change direction; ramps must be well spaced and entering volume balanced to its capacity; can be exclusive to buses/HOV.
does: Computes directional split per hour from a run or the daily curve, tests the warrant (split at least 65:35, required lanes above a threshold), and suggests which road/lane to make reversible and the switch hours; an LLM agent (extension) could switch lane direction live between demand peaks, closing the lane for a clearance interval first, like the DEVL agent.
inputs: hourly directional volumes per road (from OD routes or run), lanes, long-trip share
outputs: warrant verdict, reversal schedule (time, direction), expected delay change
existing: partial: roads can be set one-way/reversed statically; no time-of-day reversal; daily curve exists
notes: Needs a lane-direction state that changes in simulation with an all-clear interval; safe handling of vehicles on the lane when switching (amber/clearance) must be validated per AGENTS.md.

topic: Collector-distributor road to remove weaving
idea: C-D roads separate weaving from mainline: minimum lane arrangement 2 C-D + 2 core each way; transfer roads 1-2 lanes obey lane balance; terminals spaced 750 m or more from an exit ramp; C-D design speed up to 20 km/h below core; capacity and basic lane count analysed for the whole system.
does: Detects interchange clusters with heavy weaving (closely spaced entrance then exit) and proposes a parallel collector-distributor road, built with existing add_road/slip tools, then tests it by run_experiment.
inputs: interchange geometry, weaving volumes
outputs: proposed C-D layout, before/after delay
existing: partial: build_interchange (trumpet, diamond, SPUI), no C-D roads
notes: Depends on weaving analysis (weaving_check, SRC_022-009).

topic: Junction conflict point audit
idea: Fig 9-1 counts motor-vehicle conflict points: four-leg intersection 32 (16 crossing, 8 merging, 8 diverging), three-leg 9 (3 crossing, 3 merging, 3 diverging), roundabout 8 (merging and diverging only, no crossing). Recommend no more than four legs; separate driveways to reduce conflict points; conflict points also weight severity (crossing worst).
does: Static safety screen of the network: for each junction counts crossing, merging and diverging conflict points from its legs, one-way flags, lane counts, turn restrictions and control type (signal phases remove conflicts that never receive green together, roundabout has none crossing), ranks junctions, flags more than 4 legs, and estimates the reduction from converting to a roundabout or splitting a staggered pair.
inputs: junction legs, one-way roads, control type, phase groups
outputs: conflict counts by type per junction, ranking, suggested control/layout change
existing: partial: analyse_safety (post-run rear-end TTC only), set_junction_control (roundabouts)
notes: Gives the assistant a before-run, geometry-only safety figure that agrees with the roundabout safety argument and can be compared with simulated conflicts.

topic: Intersection functional area and storage
idea: The functional area of an intersection approach = perception-reaction distance + maneuver (braking and lane-change) distance + queue storage distance (Fig 9-2, 9-3); storage must hold the longest queue expected most of the time; driveways and neighbouring junctions should lie outside it; control delay is the measure for LOS and lets stop, signal and roundabout be compared (Table 9-2 LOS A-F: A very short delay, F delays unacceptable, arrival rate greater than capacity).
does: Per approach, from a run, takes the 95th percentile queue length (or the demand-capacity back-of-queue estimate) and adds the SSD/DSD and maneuver distance, compares with the road length to the upstream junction, and flags approaches where queues spill back into the previous junction or where junctions are closer than the functional area (queue blocking).
inputs: run queue data per approach, road lengths, speeds, design vehicle length
outputs: required functional length vs available, spillback frequency, flags and suggested turn-lane/storage length
existing: partial: read_detectors, analyse_run; no per-approach queue storage or spillback check
notes: Also fixes the Summary gap 'per-junction KPIs' listed in not_built.

topic: Junction level of service from control delay
idea: Intersection LOS is graded on control delay per vehicle (Table 9-2, HCM): signalised A under 10 s, B 10-20, C 20-35, D 35-55, E 55-80, F over 80; unsignalised thresholds 10/15/25/35/50 s; peak-hour basis; roundabout, stop, signal compared on delay.
does: From a run, computes mean control delay per junction and per approach (time lost versus free flow through the junction area), grades LOS A-F with the HCM thresholds for the control type, and reports the lowest-LOS approach; usable as the objective in optimise_signals and as a design target by functional class (Table 2-3).
inputs: run vehicle trajectories or per-junction crossing times, control type
outputs: per junction and approach: delay, LOS letter, v/c if known
existing: none (not_built: per-junction and per-signal KPIs, level of service)
cite: Ch 9 s9.2.5, Table 9-2 (thresholds from HCM 6th ed, not printed here)
notes: Thresholds verified against HCM 2000 (SRC_011): signalised Exhibit 16-2 (A <=10, B 10-20, C 20-35, D 35-55, E 55-80, F >80 s/veh); TWSC Exhibit 17-2 and AWSC Exhibit 17-22 (A 0-10, B 10-15, C 15-25, D 25-35, E 35-50, F >50). The Green Book's Table 9-2 itself does not print them. Requires per-vehicle junction-entry/exit timestamps, not just 5 s samples.

topic: Intersection angle and offset check
idea: Intersecting roads should meet at or near 90 degrees; at least 75 degrees gives most of the benefit; acute angles lengthen exposure time in the main flow, reduce visibility and need big turning areas; realign acute crossings by curving the minor road or by an offset intersection (two T junctions; left-then-right offset preferred over right-then-left, which needs a left-turn lane between); avoid sharp-curve connections on the side road and intersections on sharp curves; no more than 4 legs; grades near intersections under 3% (6% absolute max).
does: Computes the angle between each pair of adjacent legs of every junction (from the road end tangents), flags angles below 75 degrees (skew) and legs entering on the inside of a sharp curve, offsets between near-aligned T junctions (staggered pair spacing), and legs above 4; suggests move_junctions or an offset arrangement.
inputs: junction positions, road polylines and end tangents
outputs: per junction: leg angles, minimum angle, skew flag, stagger pairs, leg count, suggestions
existing: none (analyse_network has no angle or stagger check)
notes: Pure vector geometry; also relevant to OSM-derived networks where acute junctions and short stagger spacing abound (not_built mentions short roads in dense centres).

topic: Roundabout type and service volume check
idea: Table 9-3: mini-roundabout entry speed 25-30 km/h, inscribed diameter 13-27 m, one entry lane, up to about 15,000 veh/day; single-lane 30-40 km/h, 27-55 m, up to about 20,000 veh/day; multilane 40-50 km/h, 46-91 m, 2+ entry lanes, up to about 45,000 veh/day (two-lane) before a detailed capacity analysis; circulating speeds under 50 km/h; rotaries over 100 m and signalised circles are ineffective; neighbourhood traffic circles 15-30 m are traffic calming only.
does: For each roundabout, classifies it as mini/single/multilane from its diameter and entry lanes, compares the daily volume (from OD routing through it, hourly x 24 or the daily curve) with the Table 9-3 service-volume bound, and warns when a type is out of range (e.g. a single-lane ring with over 20,000 veh/day) or the diameter is outside the type's range; recommends type or converting to signals.
inputs: roundabout diameter, entry lanes, routed daily volume
outputs: type, volume vs bound, warnings, suggested type
existing: partial: describe (NCHRP 672 design), analyse_network (roundabouts too big for roads); not_built notes capacity only sizes demand
notes: ACMS roundabouts are one-lane ring (placeholder for multilane): the check also states the known limit.

topic: Intersection sight distance by control case (clear sight triangles)
idea: Eq 9-1 ISD = 0.278 V_major t_g (m, km/h, s). Time gaps t_g for Case B1 left turn from stop onto two-lane road: passenger car 7.5 s, single-unit truck 9.5 s, combination truck 11.5 s; right turn and Case B3 crossing about 1.0 s less (6.5 s car); +0.5 s car (+0.7 truck) per extra lane crossed (median converted to equivalent lanes, 5.5 m median = 1.5 lanes), +0.2 s per percent minor-road upgrade over 3%; decision point 4.4 m (desirably 5.4 m) back from the major road edge; example 100 km/h, 7.5 s gives 210 m (Table 9-7: 20 km/h 45 m, 50 km/h 85? ... 100 km/h 210 m); Case A (no control) legs from Table 9-4: 20 km/h 20 m, 50 km/h 45, 80 km/h 75, 100 km/h 105 (vehicles slow to about 50% of midblock speed); signal control needs only approach SSD; Case C yield; Case F left turn from major road; Case G roundabouts; skew effect.
does: For every give-way/stop/uncontrolled junction computes the required sight-triangle legs from the major-road speed and the time gap of the design manoeuvre, then tests the clear triangle against obstructions in the drawn plan (institution footprints, buildings, other roads, curve geometry) and reports blocked triangles and the speed that would be safe; reports which approaches need regulatory speed reduction or a stop control.
inputs: junction geometry, control type, major/minor road speeds, lanes, median width, institution footprints, vehicle mix
outputs: per approach: required leg lengths, available clear length, blocked flag, recommended control or speed
existing: none (no sight distance check; ACMS gap acceptance exists in simulation)
notes: Check works on the metric polyline plane; institutions already have an area and a position so they can serve as obstructions. Explains conflicts at minor approaches in analyse_safety.

topic: Critical gap values to calibrate simulated gap acceptance
idea: Field-observed accepted gaps used by AASHTO: left turn from stop 7.5 s (car), right turn 6.5 s, crossing 6.5 s (1 s less than left), trucks 9.5 and 11.5 s, +0.5 s/+0.7 s for each extra lane to cross, +0.2 s per percent upgrade; independent of major road speed; major-road drivers slow to not less than 70% of initial speed when a minor vehicle enters.
does: Measures the gaps (time headway in the conflicting stream) accepted by minor-road vehicles in a simulation run, by manoeuvre type, and compares their mean/critical value with the Green Book t_g values; also measures how much major-road traffic slows (should stay above 70%), and suggests the SUMO-style gap parameters to change.
inputs: run with junction crossing timestamps and conflict stream headways
outputs: accepted-gap distribution and estimated critical gap per manoeuvre, deviation from 7.5/6.5/6.5 s, major-road speed loss
existing: partial: check_calibration (field data validation), not_built lists 'critical gap estimation (Raff)' and 'impatience in gap acceptance'
notes: Pairs with Raff/maximum-likelihood estimators from the statistics catalogue; the values give ground truth to calibrate to.

topic: Turn-lane deceleration and storage length design
idea: Turn lane length = d1 perception-reaction (1.5 s urban, 2.5 s rural) + d2 lane change and deceleration (Table 9-20, decel 2.0 m/s2: 40 km/h 25 m, 50 35, 60 50, 70 65, 80 85, 90 105, 100 130, 110 155?, 120 185?) + d3 queue storage. Unsignalised left-turn storage: capacity c = Vo exp(-Vo tc/3600) / (1 - exp(-Vo tf/3600)) (Eq 9-3, Vo = half the two-way major flow, tc 5.0 s (50th) or 6.25 s (85th, design), tf 2.2-2.5 s) and SL = ln P(n>N) / ln(v/c) x VL (Eq 9-4, P = 0.005, VL = 7.6 m per vehicle, adjust for trucks Table 9-23); Tables 9-21/9-22 give results (e.g. 85th pct, 200 veh/h turning, 800 veh/h opposing: 23 m; 1000 veh/h: 23-61 m for higher turning volumes); minimum 16 m, 30 m high-speed/rural; signalised: 1.5-2 x average vehicles per cycle, two-lane pocket halves it; turn lanes substantially cut crashes even if short.
does: For each junction approach with a turning movement the assistant computes the required left/right turn lane length (decel plus storage) from the demand matrix routing (turn volumes), opposing flow, signal cycle/green or gap capacity, compares it with the road length and lane count, and recommends adding a lane/pocket; can then apply it as an edit and test in run_experiment.
inputs: turn volumes and opposing volume per approach (from OD route assignment), control type, signal timing, speed, truck share
outputs: per approach: capacity of the turn, required storage m, deceleration m, total length, available length, overflow probability
existing: none (turn pockets are not modelled or sized; optimise_signals tunes timing only)
notes: Needs per-approach turn flows from the routing (assign_routes / OD matrix) which ACMS has; the gap-acceptance capacity formula is the same as the HCM two-way stop capacity so can validate the simulation's measured capacity (calibrate_gap_acceptance).

topic: Unconventional intersection builders (jughandle, MUT, RCUT, displaced left turn)
idea: Indirect left-turn designs remove the left-turn phase so a signal runs two phases (shorter cycle or more arterial green): jughandle (one-way ramps in two quadrants, at least 30 m from the main stop bar, triangle about 120 x 90 m, stop control on the minor road end), loop roadway beyond the junction (radius 22.5 m min), median U-turn crossover (median at least 18 m, U-turn 120-300 m downstream, storage bay, left turns from the minor road prohibited), restricted crossing U-turn RCUT/Superstreet/J-turn (minor-road left and through movements redirected to a one-way crossover, 2 left-turn crossing conflicts and no angle crossing), displaced left turn/continuous flow (left bay to the left of oncoming traffic, midblock signal, two-phase). Suited to high major through volume, low-medium left turns, low U-turn demand; typical crash reduction 20-50% versus conventional; left-turners travel further and may stop twice.
does: Assistant tool that converts a chosen signalised or priority junction into a median-U-turn, RCUT, jughandle or displaced-left design by adding the needed roads (slip/loop roads and crossovers) and re-timing the signal to two phases, then compares it with the original through run_experiment (delay for through and left movements, stops, conflict count).
inputs: junction id, design type, crossover offset, left-turn and through volumes (from OD routing)
outputs: new roads and turn restrictions, two-phase signal plan, expected change in delay and conflict points, suitability verdict from volumes
existing: partial: add_slip_road (kerb-side turn bypass), build_interchange, set_signal_timing/optimise_signals; no indirect-left designs and no turn prohibitions at a junction
notes: Needs per-turn prohibitions and routing that honours them (assign_routes). Spacing of U-turn openings 0.4-0.8 km, 15-30 m ahead of the next left-turn lane.

topic: Roundabout entry and circulating lane adequacy thresholds
idea: Capacity rules of thumb (NCHRP 672 as quoted): one circulating lane normally carries 1,400 veh/h, up to 2,400; two-lane circulating 2,200 up to 4,000; each entry assessed separately by conflicting circulating flow: a single-lane entry is likely sufficient when entering + conflicting volume is under 1,000 veh/h (maybe 1,300), a two-lane entry when under 1,800 veh/h; design v/c 0.85-1.00; capacity best when directional split and minor share are near 0.5. Entry speed 30-40 km/h single-lane, 40-50 km/h multilane; right-turn bypass (slip) lanes raise capacity but add pedestrian/bicycle conflicts; lane continuity needs one exit lane for a through movement from a shared lane; phased design (single-lane entry first) when design-year volume is far above near-term.
does: For each roundabout entry computes the entering and conflicting (circulating) flow from the route assignment and the OD matrix at the design hour, compares the sum with the 1,000/1,300/1,800 veh/h thresholds and the 1,400 veh/h ring limit, and flags entries needing a second lane, a bypass slip road (add_slip_road) or signal control; reports the measured entry capacity from run_simulation next to it.
inputs: roundabout, approach lanes, per-entry flows (from routing), design hour
outputs: per entry: entering, conflicting, sum, verdict by threshold, recommended lanes/bypass
existing: partial: roundabout entry capacity measured on simulated drivers (capabilities), roundabout sizing (NCHRP 672), no per-entry adequacy report (not_built: 'roundabout and priority capacity only used to size demand, not reported per approach in Summary')
notes: ACMS ring is a single path (multilane placeholder): reports can state the single-lane thresholds only.

topic: Interchange warrant and benefit-cost test
idea: Six warrants for grade separation/interchange: design designation (freeway access control), bottleneck/spot congestion (capacity cannot be met at grade), crash frequency and severity, site topography, road-user benefits (benefit-cost ratio = annual road-user cost saving / annual capital cost (interest plus amortisation), above 1 minimal justification), and traffic volume (volumes beyond at-grade capacity; with equal through and cross volumes about 50% of approach traffic stops). Ramp layouts: one-quadrant for light turns, diamond for direct left turns on the minor road, cloverleaf where minor-road volume justifies; high truck share favours interchanges; crossroad access control distance needs weaving + left-turn storage + merge length.
does: Takes a junction, builds the candidate (build_interchange diamond/trumpet/SPUI) on a copy, runs paired seeds against the at-grade or signalised junction (run_experiment), converts vehicle-hours saved and stops avoided to a yearly road-user benefit using value-of-time and operating cost inputs, divides by an annualised capital cost, applies the six warrants (v/c above 1, crossing-flow share, conflict count) and gives a verdict with the benefit-cost ratio and confidence interval from the paired seeds.
inputs: junction id, interchange type, value of time per hour, vehicle operating cost per veh-km, capital cost per interchange, discount rate and life
outputs: warrant checklist, benefit, cost, B/C ratio with CI, recommendation
existing: partial: build_interchange, run_experiment (paired t-test), compare_runs; no economic appraisal
notes: Cost parameters must be user-supplied (the text gives none); the same B/C machinery serves any design alternative (signal retime, roundabout, extra lane).

topic: Lane balance, basic lanes and interchange spacing check
idea: Lane balance rules (Fig 10-52): at an entrance the lanes beyond the merge are at least (sum of lanes on the merging roadways) minus 1 and at most the sum; at an exit the approach lanes equal lanes beyond the exit plus lanes on the exit minus 1 (exception when an auxiliary lane runs between close entrance and exit under 450 m); reduce the carriageway by only one lane at a time; the basic number of lanes (design-hour volume) is held over a long stretch and local peaks are served by auxiliary lanes; minimum interchange spacing between crossroads 1.5 km urban, 3 km rural (closer only with grade-separated ramps or C-D roads); all entrances and exits on the right; one exit before the structure; uniform exit pattern along a freeway; cloverleaf is the minimum for two freeways with no at-grade left turns; simple diamond is the common freeway-to-minor-road form but limited by terminal capacity; partial cloverleaf with loops in opposite quadrants avoids weaving.
does: Walks every merge and diverge in the network (ramps, slip roads, lane drops at junctions) and tests lane counts against the lane-balance rules, finds single-lane drops of more than one lane, measures spacing between successive interchanges/crossroads on a freeway-class road, and lists violations with the corrected lane count; also suggests a diamond/trumpet/SPUI/cloverleaf from the turning volumes and the number of legs.
inputs: road graph with lanes per direction, ramps, junction legs, speeds, turning volumes
outputs: per merge/diverge: lanes in, out, rule result; spacing violations; suggested interchange type
existing: partial: analyse_network (validity, reachability); build_interchange picks lanes itself
notes: Lane drops are a classic bottleneck source in OSM-derived networks; the check pairs with the weaving and merge tools.

topic: Diverging diamond interchange builder
idea: DDI/DCD: crossroad traffic crosses to the left-hand side between the two ramp terminals so left-turn conflicts become same-direction merges and ramp terminals run two-phase signals (shorter cycle, fewer stops, shorter queues, higher left-turn capacity, fewer conflicts and shorter pedestrian crossings, retrofit cheaper than widening the bridge). Geometry: crossover design speed 30-60 km/h, reverse-curve radii 30-150 m, 15-30 m tangent between reversing curves, crossover angle 30-50 degrees (below 30 raises wrong-way risk), lane widths 3.6-4.6 m, spacing between ramp terminals governs signal design; adjacent signal spillback must be checked; not suited to oversize 'up and over' movements.
does: Extends build_interchange with a diverging diamond option that mirrors the cross road across the freeway, places the two crossover junctions with the radii/tangent/angle above, sets two-phase signal plans at both crossovers, and offers an experiment against the plain diamond (paired seeds) for delay, stops and the conflict count.
inputs: freeway road, crossroad, junction, ramp lengths, crossover radius, driving side
outputs: new network edit set, two-phase signal timing, comparison with the diamond
existing: partial: build_interchange (trumpet, diamond, SPUI; keep/replace roads, side-aware)
notes: Left-hand-side crossing means vehicles drive on the opposite side between the terminals: requires per-lane driving side handling in the router (ACMS has a global driving side).

topic: Ramp speed-change lane length and ramp spacing check
idea: Minimum acceleration lane length La (Table 10-4, flat grade, metric): highway 100 km/h and ramp controlling speed from stop 345 m, 30 km/h 305, 50 km/h 255, 60 km/h 205, 70 km/h 110; highway 80 km/h from stop 200, 50 km/h 115; 120 km/h from stop 545; merge speed Va is 74 at 100 km/h; entering driver should reach within 10 km/h of freeway speed at the convergence point; use the larger of La and gap acceptance length Lg (90-150 m); taper type 50:1 to 70:1; parallel type adds 90 m taper and at least 360 m plus taper where the merge runs near capacity; ramp curve before the lane at least 300 m radius; grade factors (Table 10-5): acceleration length x1.3-1.8 on 3-4% upgrade, x0.6-0.7 on downgrade, up to x3.5 on 5-6% upgrade; deceleration lengths in Table 10-6 (not decelerating on the main line), diverge angle 2-5 degrees. Ramp terminal spacing minimum (Fig 10-70): entrance-entrance or exit-exit 300 m (240 m with C-D road), exit-entrance 150 m (120 m), entrance-exit weaving 600 m system-to-service, 480 m service, 300 m C-D; under 450 m join as an auxiliary lane; 90 m between end of the first entrance taper and the next nose.
does: For ramps and slip roads built by the assistant (or imported), measures the acceleration/deceleration length available at each merge/diverge against Table 10-4/10-6 for the highway speed and the ramp's controlling curve speed (with grade factor), checks successive ramp terminal spacing by pair type, and flags short merges; the simulation run then reports the merge's measured speed and conflicts to confirm.
inputs: ramp geometry, highway design speed, ramp curve radii/speeds, spacing between terminals, grade
outputs: required vs available lengths, spacing violations, suggested ramp lengthening or auxiliary lane
existing: partial: build_interchange (trumpet/diamond/SPUI geometry, curve_speed_kmh); no length criteria
notes: Table 10-4 follows from kinematics (a about 1.0-1.5 m/s2 from initial speed to merge speed), so values can be computed rather than stored; the lookup is the check.

topic: Ramp metering as a signal override/agent
idea: Ramp metering regulates entrance-ramp inflow with signals before the entrance terminal to balance freeway demand and capacity, smooth stop-and-go and reduce crashes: pretimed (regular headway from studies), traffic-actuated from mainline and ramp detectors (local or corridor-wide algorithms), releasing vehicles singly or in two-vehicle platoons, or gap-based release matched to a detected mainline gap; can be tied to HOV bypass lanes.
does: An extension (signal_override hook) for entrance ramps built by build_interchange or add_slip_road: a meter signal with a release rate set from downstream mainline occupancy/speed (a feedback rule such as ALINEA r(k)=r(k-1)+K(target_occupancy - measured)), with min/max rate and queue override so the ramp queue does not spill onto the crossroad; the assistant (or an LLM agent) can pick the rate policy and the experiment compares delay and mainline speed with and without.
inputs: entrance ramp, downstream detector (mainline occupancy/speed), target occupancy, rate bounds, queue-length limit
outputs: metering plan, simulated mainline throughput, speed and ramp delay with/without
existing: partial: extensions can override signals (TSP, DEVL); SCATS/SCOOT adaptive timing from loop detectors; no ramp metering
notes: The ALINEA law and K gain are from the ramp-metering literature, not in this text; the text gives goals, modes and platoon release. Needs the ramp to be a signalled single-lane approach (stop line) which add_slip_road gives.

topic: Driver path test for interchange complexity
idea: Test each principal origin-destination path through a freeway/interchange sequence from the driver's view: only the road being travelled, its exits/entrances, signs, peak-hour volumes, lanes and speeds; weaknesses (exits too close, successive weaving sections, lane changes through the freeway such as left merge then right diverge, unsignable layouts) show up per path; desirable solution has no lane changes on the through lanes (Fig 10-80, 1.5-5 km between branch connection and fork).
does: For every OD route (or the busiest ones) counts decision points per km (exits, forks, merges), forced lane changes, weaving sections crossed, left-side exits, and minimum spacing between consecutive decisions against decision sight distance, producing a per-route complexity score and listing the worst interchange spots.
inputs: routes from assign_routes/OD matrix, junction and ramp topology, lanes
outputs: per route: decision points, lane changes needed, spacing violations, score; per junction: routes burdened
existing: partial: critical_links (route redundancy), network_indices, assign_routes; no per-route decision complexity
notes: Also explains lane-changing failures (LC2013 missed exits) seen in a run: join to read_traffic routes.

topic: Design-practice benchmarks for validating simulated behaviour
idea: The Green Book fixes numeric behaviour anchors that a microsimulation can be tested against: brake reaction 2.5 s design (0.64 s alerted median, +1 s unexpected), comfortable braking 3.4 m/s2 (90% of drivers brake harder than 3.4, most above 4.5), deceleration into turn lanes 2.0 m/s2 (two-thirds of drivers), lateral accel f 0.15-0.4 by speed, vehicles slow to about 50% of midblock speed at uncontrolled junctions (1.5 m/s2), critical gaps 7.5/6.5/6.5 s (left/right/cross) and tc 5.0-6.25 s with follow-up 2.2-2.5 s, double left-turn lane about 195% of a single lane, roundabout single-lane entry ok under 1,000 veh/h entering+conflicting, pedestrians 1.1 m/s, truck speed loss 15 km/h on critical grade length, 2-3 mph speed loss per signal per mile.
does: A fixed suite of small headless scenarios (straight stop, uncontrolled approach, stop-controlled left turn, double left lane, roundabout entry, signal discharge) that measures the simulation's emergent value for each anchor and reports pass/fail with tolerances, so a change to vehicle.py or simulation.py is regression-tested against design practice.
inputs: benchmark scenario set, tolerances
outputs: table of anchor, source value, simulated value, deviation, verdict
existing: partial: check_calibration (field counts), tests/ (unit tests), not a design-practice anchor suite
notes: Values scattered across the text; compile once into docs/architecture/sources.md for the assistant to cite.
